sections.heading: Dialogue III, Knot xvi, part 1 (printed pp. 402–411)
rows: [Margin, p. 402: Nodus XVI. Cur res humanae videantur casu geri.]
[Margin, p. 402: Knot XVI. Why human affairs seem to be carried on [geri] by chance [casu].]

Asphal. Hanc itaque non levem querelam hominum mitiga, quod cum homo rationalis sit, nihil tamen fere secundum rationem geritur. Neque artificum esse gratiam, neque fortium bellum, neque sapientium panem. Sed tempus & casum ubique dominari, conqueritur quo nemo sapientior extitit. Quomodo itaque recte gubernatur orbis & ad hominum naturam? cum quasi sponte sua & casu ferantur etiam haec quae homines proxime spectant. Neque fas est causari haec hominum ipsorum esse gesta, & eorum vitio fieri, si enim ipsa eorum natura secus quam oportebat, ordinata est, quid de caeteris sperari potest?

Asphal. This therefore not light complaint of men soothe [mitiga]: that, although man is rational, nothing however nearly [fere] is carried on [geritur] according to reason. [That] neither is there favour [gratiam] to craftsmen [artificum], nor war to the strong, nor bread to the wise; but [that] time and chance [casum] rule everywhere, complains he than whom no one wiser has stood forth [extitit]. How therefore is the world [orbis] rightly governed, and according to [ad] the nature of men? since as if of their own accord [sponte sua] and by chance are borne even these [things] which most nearly [proxime] regard men. Nor is it right [fas] to plead [causari] that these are the doings [gesta] of men themselves, and come about by their fault [vitio]; for if their very nature has been ordered otherwise than it ought, what can be hoped concerning the rest?

Ereu. In latum me quaestionum Pelagus vocas. Sed ut facilius sulcemus ignotum aequor, figenda nobis est prora in plagam, quam fugientem sequimur: ut ab ipsa cursus post modum ratio foelicius agnoscatur. Hoc itaque vides manifestum esse ut quoniam homo finis est, mundus hic, id est, telluris pontique globus non potuerit aptius ordinari, quam quomodo huic generi maxime est idoneus, & quod non tam sequitur quam praeit, non potuisse Deum, si optimum semper facit, non hominem optimum creavisse, & quod huic connexum est, hunc quem habemus ordinem caeteris praeferendum, hunc dico, quem tu calumniaris.

Ereu. Into a wide Sea [Pelagus] of questions you call me. But that we may more easily furrow [sulcemus] the unknown expanse [aequor], the prow must be fixed by us toward the region [plagam] which, [as it is] fleeing, we follow: that from it itself the reason [ratio] of the course may afterwards [post modum] be more happily [foelicius] recognised. This therefore you see to be manifest: that, since man is the end [finis], this world, that is, the globe of earth [telluris] and sea [ponti], could not have been ordered more fitly than in the way in which it is most suited to this kind [generi]; and, what does not so much follow as go before [praeit], that God could not, if He always makes the best, not have created man best; and, what is connected to this, that this order which we have [is] to be preferred to the others, this [one], I say, which you calumniate.
[Margin, p. 403: Ex natura hominum esse ut mundus sit qualis est.]
[Margin, p. 403: That it is from the nature of men that the world is such as it is.]

Asphal. Iam haec sciebam. Sed nisi ipsi speciatim humano generi convenire hanc rerum gestarum seriem docueris, nihil efficis. Ex eo enim quod experimur male geri rem humanam, iisdem vestigiis omnia retro agentur quibus ea hactenus perduxisti.

Asphal. These [things] I knew already. But unless you shall have taught that this series of things done [rerum gestarum] suits the human kind itself specifically [speciatim], you effect nothing. For from this, that we experience the human affair [rem humanam] to be carried on badly, all [things] will be driven back [retro agentur] by the same footsteps by which you have hitherto led them through [perduxisti].
Ereu. Age igitur, homo cum corpore constet & anima, tanquam partibus componentibus, credisne aliquam harum potuisse fieri meliorem, substantialiter dico & non secundum accidens?

Ereu. Come then: since man consists of body and soul, as of component parts, do you believe that any [aliquam] of these could have been made better, substantially [substantialiter], I say, and not according to accident [secundum accidens]?

Asphal. Non potest: si enim anima melior foret, non eadem foret; neque nos homines essemus; sed aliud aliquod animalium genus nostro loco suppositum: Formae enim diversitas speciei varietatem inducit. Si autem eidem animae alterius speciei corpus indueretur, uti illo non posset magis quam ars tibiis canendi, testudine vel cithara. Est enim quod ars ad organum, hoc forma ad materiam, anima ad corpus, correctis quibusdam accidentibus.

Asphal. It cannot: for if the soul were better, it would not be the same; nor would we be men, but some other kind of animals put under [suppositum] in our place: for diversity of form brings in [inducit] variety of species. But if on the same soul a body of another species were put [indueretur], it could not use it more than the art of playing [canendi] on pipes [tibiis] [could use] a tortoise-shell lyre [testudine] or a cithara. For what art is to [its] instrument [organum], this form is to matter, soul to body, certain accidents being corrected [correctis].
Ereu. His ita accommodatis, quid de cerebro putas, non ipsum esse immediatum animae motorem, & quod hinc fit, potissimum animae organum?

Ereu. These [things] being so fitted [accommodatis], what do you think of the brain: [is it] not itself the immediate mover [motorem] of the soul [animae], and, what follows from this [quod hinc fit], the chief [potissimum] instrument [organum] of the soul?

Asphal. Assentior. Cottidianis enim monemur eventis nihil nos sine phantasmatum excitatione intelligere, neque novi neque praecogniti, haec autem cerebri quosdam incolas esse pari constantia scitum est.

Asphal. I assent. For by daily events we are reminded [monemur] that we understand nothing without the excitation of phantasms [phantasmatum], neither [of anything] new nor [of anything] foreknown [praecogniti]; and that these are certain inhabitants of the brain is known [scitum est] with equal constancy.
Ereu. Num itaque cerebrum homini melius potuisse dari credis?
Ereu. Do you then believe [num] that a better brain could have been given to man?

Asphal. Nequaquam: tantumdem enim foret aliud corpus atque aliud cerebrum largiri, cum cerebrum illud sit quo immediate utitur animus ad caetera: si itaque non alio corpore uti potest, neque alio cerebro utetur.

Asphal. By no means: for it would be just as much [tantumdem] to bestow another body as another brain, since the brain is that which the mind [animus] uses immediately for the rest: if therefore it cannot use another body, neither will it use another brain.

Ereu. Et tali cerebro tale cor, tali cordi tales pulmones & iecur necessaria sunt, his autem totum reliqui corporis cataphragma & vestitus. Non potuit itaque horum omnium alia fuisse ratio. Et quoniam talibus membris tale nutrimentum inservit, & iis quibus alitur & vestitur homo, tellus, & aqua, & aer quae nos circumvallant, haec etiam omnia non potuerunt esse alia; & quoniam ex his ortum habent mixta, Plantae & animalia quae praeter hominem sunt, haec etiam eadem esse debuerant. Haec autem ea fere omnia complectuntur, quae per sensuum ministeria impellunt cogitationem & propensionem humanam. Quare & motiva sensuum & disciplinae quae ex iis pendent, ex natura generis humani sunt, neque alia esse potuerunt.

Ereu. And to such a brain such a heart, to such a heart such lungs and liver are necessary, and to these the whole covering-armour [cataphragma] and clothing of the rest of the body. There could not therefore have been another reason [ratio] of all these. And since to such members such nourishment is serviceable [inservit], and [since] to those [things] by which man is nourished and clothed [are serviceable] the earth [tellus], and water, and air, which wall us around [circumvallant], these also all could not be other; and since from these the mixed [bodies] [mixta] have [their] origin, the Plants and animals which are besides man, these also had to be [debuerant] the same. And these embrace nearly all those [things] which through the ministries of the senses impel human thought and propension [propensionem]. Wherefore both the motives [motiva] of the senses and the disciplines which depend on them are from the nature of the human kind, nor could they have been other.

Asphal. Cito res magnas expedis. Verum quis tibi concesserit animalium species alias non posse esse humano generi, si non magis, certe non minus congruas, & cum aliquae species magis ex materiei qualitate, quam ex hominis intuitu procreentur, cur asserendum est vel alias aliquando non fuisse, vel non posse esse, vel non iterum futuras?

Asphal. Quickly you dispatch [expedis] great things. But who would grant you that other species of animals cannot be, if not more, certainly not less congruous to the human kind; and, since some species are procreated more from the quality of the matter [materiei] than from regard [intuitu] to man, why is it to be asserted either that others have not at some time been, or cannot be, or will not again be [futuras]?

Ereu. Probe intelligis. Neque ego de animalium speciebus: Sed de generibus locutus sum. Quo enim ab homine longius disceditur, eo par est latiores esse rerum differentias quae ex necessitate eum comitantur. Et sic ipso usu videmus non easdem vel herbarum vel animalium species in omnibus regionibus nasci, etsi per analogiam omnia ubique sint. Sed ut efficiam hoc quo tendebam, illud mihi dicendum erat super, quod cum prudentia humana vel ex corporis humani temperie vel ex disciplina ortum habeat, quae utraque ex ipsa naturae indole certam & terminatam regulam accepisse cernimus: conficitur eandem quae est, ut sit ab ipsa natura haberi, neque ut sapientiores homines existerent, nisi mutata natura, contingere potuisse: & proinde, quod experimur, ex natura esse, ut longe maior hominum pars imprudentia condemnetur. Quoniam autem non leve est in hoc dicto ad querelas tuas sopiendas momentum, libet hunc nodum fortius aliquantulum astringere. Dic itaque mihi in quo putes prudentiam humanam sitam esse?

Ereu. You understand rightly. Neither did I [speak] of the species of animals, but of the kinds [generibus] I spoke. For the further one departs [disceditur] from man, by so much it is fitting [par est] that the differences of things be wider which from necessity accompany him. And so by use itself we see that not the same species either of herbs or of animals are born in all regions, although by analogy [per analogiam] all [things] are everywhere. But that I may effect this whither I was tending, that remained [super] to be said by me: that, since human prudence has [its] origin either from the temperament [temperie] of the human body or from discipline, each of which we perceive to have received a certain and terminated [terminatam] rule from the very disposition [indole] of nature, it is concluded [conficitur] that the same [prudence] which there is, such as it is [ut sit], is had from nature itself, and that it could not have happened that men should exist wiser, unless nature were changed; and therefore, what we experience, [that] it is from nature that by far the greater part of men is condemned by imprudence [imprudentia]. But since [it is] not a light moment [momentum] [that] there is in this saying for lulling your complaints to sleep [sopiendas], it pleases [me] to tighten this knot [nodum] somewhat more strongly. Tell me therefore in what you think human prudence is placed [sitam]?
[Margin, p. 406: plerosque ex naturae lege esse imprudentes.]
[Margin, p. 406: that most [men] are imprudent from the law of nature.]

Asphal. In clara quadam, & imperturbata rerum singularum perceptione. Video enim communes rationes omnium ad regulas, hoc est, scientias vel artes redigi posse, ad prudentiam itaque singularium inspectio & iudicium pertinebit: Iudicium autem omne in claritate & quiete situm esse omnis experientia testatur: est enim finis motus qui animum ex dubietate seu perturbatione ad quietem & claritatem perducit.

Asphal. In a certain clear and unperturbed perception of singular things. For I see that the common reasons [rationes] of all [things] can be reduced to rules, that is, to sciences or arts; to prudence therefore will pertain the inspection and judgement of singulars. But that every judgement is placed in clearness and quiet, all experience testifies: for it is the end of the motion which leads the mind [animum] through from doubtfulness or perturbation to quiet and clearness.
Ereu. Imprudentia ergo in quo?
Ereu. Imprudence then, in what?
Asphal. In iudicio de singularibus quoque, sed non claro & perturbato.
Asphal. In judgement about singulars also, but [judgement] not clear and perturbed.
Ereu. Quid autem facit iudicium perturbatum?
Ereu. And what makes judgement perturbed?
Asphal. Cum intellectus alieno motu cogitur ad ferendam sententiam antequam dilucescat satis: hoc autem ex passione plerumque ei contingit.
Asphal. When the intellect is driven [cogitur] by another's [alieno] motion to bring [ferendam] a verdict [sententiam] before it dawns [dilucescat] enough: and this happens to it mostly from passion.
Ereu. Quid ergo? hominem sine passione vivere posse credis?
Ereu. What then? do you believe that a man can live without passion?
Asphal. Magni viri crediderunt, sed quoniam etiam a non minoribus contradicitur: an aliquam evidentiam afferre valeas scire aveo.
Asphal. Great men have believed [so]; but since it is also contradicted by not lesser [men], I long [aveo] to know whether you are able to bring some evidence [evidentiam].
Ereu. Ego evidentiae impar sum, nisi ubi res ipsa sese offert. Quid enim putas esse passionem?
Ereu. I am unequal to evidence, except where the thing itself offers itself. For what do you think passion to be?
Asphal. Evidentem & impetuosum appetitus sensitivi motum.
Asphal. An evident and impetuous motion of the sensitive appetite [appetitus sensitivi].
Ereu. Differt itaque a levi motu appetitus sensitivi sola τῷ magis & minus differentia. Si itaque omnes animales actus nostri, appetitus sensitivi beneficio perficiuntur, quid opinaris?

Ereu. It differs therefore from a light motion of the sensitive appetite by the sole difference of the ‘more and less’ [τῷ magis & minus]. If therefore all our animal acts are accomplished by the benefit of the sensitive appetite, what do you opine?
Asphal. Iam non opinor, sed scio nisi de nomine fiat quaestio, omnino impossibile esse hominem sine passione existere.
Asphal. Now I do not opine, but I know, unless the question be made about the name, that it is altogether impossible that a man exist without passion.

Ereu. In moderatione itaque passionum consistit prudentia. Passiones vero contrariae sunt: contrariorum autem moderatio in medio consistit: medium autem invenire non esse facile; sed artis negotium docet Philosophus. Sed ad nos quod spectat, est, minores esse differentias quo magis ad medium acceditur, latiores vero quo magis receditur. Ex quo evidens rursus est, naturam seu causas naturales contingentes latiorem campum habere errandi a medio, in quo consistit sive prudentia sive vicinia prudentiae, quam illud attingendi: & quod hinc fit, non minori necessitate ex naturali dispositione longe plures esse imprudentes qui passioni alicui vel pluribus subiecti sunt, quam prudentes qui omnibus liberi sunt: ut non immerito stultorum esse plena omnia pronunciatum sit. Quantula enim hominum pars per disciplinas emendatior fit, loquantur Academiae in quibus quota hominum pars versatur, videmus, & ex ea rursus parte quota prudentiam discat, non sustineo declarare, ne lapidationem mihi promeream. His modo si acquiescis, ad dolorem tuum leniendum me accingo.

Ereu. In the moderation therefore of the passions consists prudence. But the passions are contrary; and the moderation of contraries consists in the mean [medio]; and that to find the mean is not easy, but [is] the business of art, the Philosopher teaches. But what regards us is [this]: that the differences are smaller the more one approaches [acceditur] to the mean, but wider the more one recedes. From which again it is evident that nature, or natural contingent causes, have a wider field for erring from the mean, in which consists either prudence or the vicinity of prudence, than for attaining it; and, what follows from this [quod hinc fit], [that] by no lesser necessity from natural disposition far more are imprudent, who are subject to some one passion or to more, than prudent, who are free from all: so that not undeservedly it has been pronounced that all [things] are full of fools. For how small [quantula] a part of men becomes more amended [emendatior] through disciplines, let the Academies [Academiae] speak; in which what fraction [quota] of men is engaged [versatur], we see; and from that part again what fraction learns prudence, I do not venture [sustineo] to declare, lest I earn stoning for myself. If only you acquiesce in these [things], I gird myself for soothing your pain.
Asphal. Pergito.
Asphal. Proceed [pergito].

Ereu. Hoc ergo, ut credo, nihil dubitas omnium scientiarum & artium applicatricem & quasi dominam & gubernatricem esse prudentiam, non dico eam quae ad singulas artes requiritur, quarum species sunt Militaris, Iuridica, Regalis & similes, sed eam quae toti hominum vitae consulit & actionis humanae ut humanae arbitra est. Haec ducem an suscipiendum sit imperium docet: iudicem, ne quid cupiditate vel odio agat. Omnem denique artificem gubernat, ut artem vitae suae accommodet. Dirigamus nunc eo orationem ut cur artificum non sit gratia, videamus? Gratiam esse artificum tunc dicimus cum pro merito artis aestimatur. Quod autem non aestimetur iuxta peritiam suam vel ex ipso potest pendere, vel ex iis a quibus aestimandus foret. Ipse sibi contemptus causa est, si artem suam iis quae minus aestimanda sunt, posthabet: Si potestatem, pecuniam, voluptatem adoret: & a quibus sibi supplicari debeat, iis sese dictorum ergo submittat. Rursus si contemptoribus importune sese ingerat, neque horas quibus alii captari debent, observet. Ab aliis contemptus oritur, cum ignari ipsi ex ignarorum ore artificia & artificem expendunt. Unde loco periti artificis obtruditur necessarius alicuius familiaris, vel adulator aliquis, & denique quisquis artifex non ex artis merito, sed personae conditione praefertur. Utramque causam expende: habes imprudentiam; confer cum dictis. Et si necesse sit, & ex generis humani qualitate; ut imprudentium excedat multitudo; confectum habes etiam secundum naturam hominis esse ut artificum non sit gratia; sed opportunitas, & causae per accidens obtineant, discussis iis quae gratiam facere per se nata sunt. Quod de artificum gratia tantumdem de reliquis, de quibus querela fit, exemplo ducto facile conficitur, ut ea sic usuvenire secundum conditionem humanae naturae esse appareat. Quid itaque conquerendum habemus? num quod homines sumus? quod secundum naturam gubernamur? Quid itaque Deum fecisse volumus? Naturamne immutare iubemus? Sed ratio mandat ut si aliter gubernare velit, aliam naturam cui hoc consentaneum sit, eligat; ut sectioni serram, vel securim, percussioni malleum, situlam aquae hauriendae non cribrum quod oppletis poris opus habet, adhibemus. Sic unumquodque operi cui natum est, & opus ei quod ad illud natum est, attribuere iustum est. Vis fortassis ut causas naturales mutet? Primo supra vel contra naturam non secundum eam faciet, nos autem Philosophos agimus. Deinde non debuit mutandas seligere, vel si alias non potuit, iis quod optimae essent, contentus esse.

Ereu. This then, as I believe, you in no way doubt: that prudence is the applier [applicatricem] and as it were the mistress and governess of all sciences and arts; I do not mean that [prudence] which is required for the single arts, whose species are the Military, the Juridical, the Regal and the like, but that which takes counsel [consulit] for the whole life of men and is arbiter of human action as human. This teaches the commander [ducem] whether command [imperium] is to be undertaken; the judge, lest he do anything from desire or hatred. Every craftsman [artificem], finally, it governs, that he may accommodate [his] art to his life. Shall we now direct [our] discourse [orationem] thither, that we may see why there is not favour [gratia] to craftsmen? We say there is favour to craftsmen then, when [a craftsman] is esteemed according to the merit of [his] art. But that he is not esteemed according to his skill [peritiam] can depend either on himself, or on those by whom he ought [foret] to be esteemed. He himself is the cause of contempt to himself, if he puts his art after [posthabet] those [things] which are less to be esteemed: if he adores power, money, pleasure; and to those by whom he ought to be supplicated, to them submits himself for the sake [ergo] of the [things] said. Again, if he thrusts himself importunately on despisers, nor observes the hours at which others ought to be caught [captari]. From others contempt arises, when [men] themselves ignorant weigh [expendunt] works of art [artificia] and the craftsman from the mouth of the ignorant. Whence in the place of the skilled craftsman is thrust in a kinsman [necessarius] of some intimate [familiaris], or some flatterer; and finally whatever craftsman is preferred not from the merit of [his] art, but from the condition of [his] person. Weigh both causes: you have imprudence; compare [it] with the [things] said. And if it be necessary, and [that] from the quality of the human kind, that the multitude of the imprudent exceed, you have [it] concluded [confectum] also that it is according to the nature of man that there is not favour to craftsmen, but [that] opportunity and causes by accident [per accidens] prevail [obtineant], those being shaken off [discussis] which are born [nata sunt] to make favour by themselves [per se]. What [holds] of the favour of craftsmen, just as much [tantumdem] of the rest, about which complaint is made, is easily concluded [conficitur], the example being drawn [exemplo ducto], so that it appears that it is according to the condition of human nature that they so come about [usuvenire]. What therefore have we to complain of? [is it] that we are men? that we are governed according to nature? What therefore do we wish God to have done? Do we bid [him] change nature? But reason commands that, if he should wish to govern otherwise, he choose another nature, to which this is consonant [consentaneum]; as for cutting we apply a saw or an axe, for striking a hammer, for drawing water a bucket, not a sieve, which has need of [its] pores filled up. So it is just to attribute each thing to the work for which it is born [natum], and to [each thing] the work which is born [natum] for it. Do you perhaps wish that he change natural causes? First, he will act above or against nature, not according to it; and we are acting [the part of] Philosophers. Then, he ought not to have chosen [causes] to be changed, or, if he could not [choose] others, [ought] to be content with these, because they were the best.
Asphal. Video quae dicis ex ratione esse, neque quid responsem habeo. Nescio quid tamen intus angit, neque sicut soleo, plene acquiesco.
Asphal. I see that what you say is from reason, nor have I anything to answer [responsem]. I know not what, however, distresses [angit] [me] within, nor, as I am wont, do I fully acquiesce.

Ereu. Vatem me dicito si diviner. Homo es, & homini non optime esse male te habet. Dignum scilicet eum existimas cuius causa adamantinae causarum series & necessitatis ferreae portae effringantur: Neque acceptas quamcumque causam pro legitima, quae contra eam ferat. Inde remorderis, inde sollicitus es & laboras.

Ereu. Call me a prophet [vatem] if I divine [diviner]. You are a man, and that it is not best [optime] with man holds you badly [male te habet]. Worthy, namely [scilicet], you deem him, for whose cause [causa] the adamantine series of causes and the iron gates of necessity should be broken open [effringantur]; nor do you accept any cause [causam] as legitimate which bears [ferat] against it [eam]. Hence you are gnawed [remorderis], hence you are anxious and labour.
[Margin, p. 410: Mundus propter quos creatus sit?]
[Margin, p. 410: For whose sake [propter quos] was the world created?]

Asphal. Non omnino abhorreo rem se habere ut dicis. Verum utcumque sit, ab ea querela desisto, sed sic ut subiiciam aliam, quae fere omnium bonorum est & fuit. Mundum hunc hominis bono addictum affirmas. Esto, sed cuius hominum partis? bonorum an improborum? si bonorum cur non perfruuntur? hos enim abiectos, miseros, poenis & doloribus saturatos videmus. Malorum? at refugit animus credere: quantumvis eadem ratione videatur consistere qua hominibus natum hunc orbem confecisti: si enim providentia & voluntate Dei fiunt quae fiunt omnia; factum autem videmus ut mali plerumque potestate emineant, honoribus clarescant, divitiis affluant, voluptatibus diffluant: quid ultra loquimur, nisi ut in eorum gratiam haec facta arbitremur? Vide modo tu, quomodo cum tali gubernatore omnium potente ipso sapientiae fonte, ipso bonitatis ubere, talis gubernatio consistere possit, ut credi tibi ab his qui demonstrationi tuae sunt impares, assequaris.

Asphal. I do not altogether shrink [abhorreo] [from] the thing holding itself as you say. But however it be, from that complaint I desist, but so that I subjoin another, which is and was [the complaint] of nearly all good [men]. You affirm this world [to be] made over [addictum] to the good of man. Be it so; but to which part of men? of the good or of the wicked? if of the good, why do they not enjoy [it] fully [perfruuntur]? for these we see cast down, wretched, sated with punishments and griefs. Of the bad? but the mind flees back [refugit] from believing [it]: however much it may seem to stand [consistere] by the same reason by which you concluded [confecisti] this world [orbem] born for men. For if by the providence and will of God all [things] that come about come about; and we see it come about [factum] that the bad mostly are eminent in power, grow bright with honours, flow with riches, flow apart [diffluant] in pleasures: what further are we saying, except that we judge these [things] done in their favour [gratiam]? See only you, how, with such a governor, powerful over all [omnium potente], the very fountain of wisdom, the very udder [ubere] of goodness, such a governance can stand [consistere], so that you may obtain [assequaris] to be believed by those who are unequal to your demonstration.

terms: Cur res humanae videantur casu geri
Why human affairs seem to be carried on by chance
be done, be managed; happen by chance
Title of the knot; casus = chance (glossary). Res gerere is the standard idiom for conducting affairs, hence res gestae = ‘things done’.
Neque artificum esse gratiam, neque fortium bellum, neque sapientium panem … tempus & casum
neither favour to craftsmen, nor war to the strong, nor bread to the wise … time and chance
gratia = favour, popularity, success; bellum = (victory in) war

Ecclesiastes 9:11 (Vulgate: ‘nec velocium esse cursum, nec fortium bellum, nec sapientium panem … nec artificum gratiam, sed tempus casumque in omnibus’). ‘He than whom no one wiser has stood forth’ = Solomon, the traditional author (cf. 1 Kings 3:12).
White defines it on p. 408: being valued according to the merit of one's art. Glossary rendering ‘favour’ kept.
Covers any skilled art (incl. liberal ones); glossary ‘craftsman’ kept.
Kept distinct from mundus where it is printed (glossary).
according to [ad] the nature of men
Asks whether the world is governed in a way fitted to human nature.
allege as cause; make an excuse
Classical ‘to plead as excuse’; also plays on causa.
open sea; level surface; plough; quarter of the sky
Extended nautical metaphor (Virgilian diction: sulcare aequor, Aen. 5.158). The region ‘which, fleeing, we follow’ is the receding horizon.
the globe of earth and sea
White's standing distinction: the ‘world’ ordered for man is the earth-sea globe, not the whole universe.
quod non tam sequitur quam praeit
what does not so much follow as go before
is not so much a consequence as a premise
Logical idiom: the point is prior to, not derived from, what was said.
the human affair / series of things done
will be driven back … by the same footsteps
The argument will be retraced backwards (from bad effects to a bad cause).
Scholastic: better in its essence vs. better in some accidental quality.
Here participle ‘substituted in our place’, with an overtone of the scholastic term.
diversity of form brings in variety of species
Aristotelian-Thomist principle: the substantial form gives the species, so a different soul is a different species.
be clothed with; be put on
Body as garment of the soul; ‘art of singing with pipes … tortoise-shell or cithara’ echoes Aristotle, De anima I.3, 407b25 (each art must use its own instruments).
tortoise; lyre (made of tortoise-shell); siege shelter
Classical poetic word for the lyre.
Glossary ‘instrument’; the brain as the soul's principal organ.
with allowance made for certain accidental differences
The analogy art:instrument :: form:matter holds with qualifications.
the immediate mover of the soul
the soul's immediate mover (i.e. the mover the soul uses)
Genitive ambiguous: objective (moves the soul) or possessive (the soul's own moving instrument). The context (the soul uses the brain immediately) favours the latter.
Aristotelian ‘no understanding without a phantasm’ (De anima III.7, 431a16), conversio ad phantasmata; White and Digby place phantasms physically in the brain.
Glossary distinction kept: animus = mind, anima = soul.
coat of mail; protective covering; (anat.) diaphragm (rare)
Greek κατάφραγμα, armour; here the body's outer coverings (skin, flesh, bones) that protect the inner organs. The anatomical sense ‘diaphragm’ is possible but less likely with vestitus.
Aristotelian mixta: bodies compounded of the elements (glossary).
Final-cause idiom: produced with a view to man.
White grants variation of species but holds the kinds (genera) of creatures fixed by man's nature.
Each region has analogous (not identical) creatures.
it is concluded / you have [it] concluded / you concluded
Logical sense of conficere = to establish a conclusion (Ciceronian).
Pun on nodus, White's name for his sections (‘knots’).
Aristotelian phronesis concerns particulars (Nic. Eth. VI.7–8), whereas science and art deal with universals (rationes communes).
Judicial metaphor; the intellect forced to judge before light is sufficient.
Here ‘evident and impetuous motion of the sensitive appetite’, the scholastic definition (cf. Aquinas, ST I-II q.22).
Scholastic faculty, divided into concupiscible and irascible.
Aristotelian formula: things differing by ‘more and less’ do not differ in kind (Categories 5, 4a; Physics).
Nicomachean Ethics II.9, 1109a24–26: to find the mean is a task (ergon), not easy. ‘The Philosopher’ = Aristotle in scholastic usage.
Contingent causes miss the mean more often than they hit it, since the mean is one and the deviations are many.
all things are full of fools
Proverb: Cicero, Ad familiares 9.22.4 (‘stultorum plena sunt omnia’).
Prudence as architectonic virtue directing arts and sciences to life (cf. Nic. Eth. VI; Aquinas, prudentia as auriga virtutum).
Aristotle's species of prudence (Nic. Eth. VI.8: legislative, political, economic); White calls them prudences of particular arts.
for the sake of the [things] said
on account of the aforesaid (power, money, pleasure)
Archaic ergo + genitive = ‘for the sake of’.
Scholastic causal distinction: favour should come from merit (per se cause) but comes from opportunity (per accidens causes).
supra vel contra naturam / secundum naturam
above or against nature / according to nature
Scholastic triad for divine action; White insists the philosopher treats only what is according to nature.
we are acting [the part of] Philosophers
agere + role = to play a part.
Rare; read as quid responsem habeo, ‘what I should answer’.
call me a prophet if I divine
Poetic image of fate (cf. Virgil, Aen. 6.552 ‘porta adversa ingens solidoque adamante columnae’; Horace, Odes 3.24.5–8, Necessitas with adamantine nails).
Wordplay: ‘for whose cause’ (sake), the ‘series of causes’, and ‘any cause as legitimate’ (forensic sense, a case/plea).
Roman-law term for handing over property.
dissolve, melt away (in pleasures); be dissipated
Classical: ‘luxuria diffluere’ (Terence, Cicero); pun with affluant.
notes: Unit: Dialogue III, Knot xvi, part 1 of an estimated 3. PDF pp. 413–422 = printed pp. 402–411, from Asphalius' ‘Hanc itaque non levem querelam…’ (p. 402, beside the margin ‘Nodus XVI. Cur res humanae videantur casu geri’) to the end of Asphalius' speech ‘…assequaris.’ (p. 411). Offset +11 holds (running heads 402–411; signatures Eee ij p. 403, Eee iij p. 405, Fff p. 409, Fff ij p. 411). Part 2 begins on p. 411 (PDF 422) with Ereunius' ‘Ego vero quod in me est libens exequar.’ Knot XVII starts p. 424 per the table.

Uncertain / suspect readings (all clear in the print): (1) p. 405 ‘conficitur eandem quae est, ut sit ab ipsa natura haberi’ — the construction is awkward (ut sit ‘such as it is’ inserted into an accusative-and-infinitive); translated literally. (2) p. 410 ‘quae contra eam ferat’ — eam has no clear feminine antecedent other than causa (‘for whose cause’), i.e. man's case; translated ‘against it’. (3) p. 410 ‘responsem’ — rare subjunctive of responso, kept. (4) p. 403 ‘immediatum animae motorem’ — the genitive is ambiguous (see terms). No {?} or {illeg.} readings in this part.

Interpretive choices: (a) p. 402 the infinitives ‘esse … dominari’ depend on conqueritur (Solomon complains), so the quotation of Eccl. 9:11 is reported speech; bracketed [That]. (b) p. 404 ‘& iis quibus alitur … tellus, & aqua, & aer’ — inservit understood again: the elements serve the things that feed and clothe man. (c) p. 405 ‘imprudentia condemnetur’ — ablative, rendered ‘condemned by imprudence’ (i.e. sentenced to it by nature). (d) p. 409 ‘tantumdem de reliquis’ — understood ‘[holds] of the rest’.

Verification pass: the Latin was re-read sentence by sentence against the page images and the English. Corrections made: 3 — (a) p. 406 ‘non leve est … momentum’ first rendered ‘there is no light moment’, corrected to keep the litotes ‘[it is] not a light moment’; (b) p. 403 ‘ars tibiis canendi’ first ‘the art of singing with pipes’, corrected to ‘playing on pipes’ (canere tibiis = play the pipe); (c) p. 411 ‘tali gubernatore omnium potente’ first split as ‘governor of all, powerful’, corrected to ‘powerful over all’ (omnium potens, cf. omnipotens). Also checked and confirmed: future ‘utetur’ (‘will it use’, p. 404), future perfect ‘docueris’ (p. 403), pluperfect ‘debuerant’ (‘had to be’, p. 404), fugientem agreeing with plagam (p. 402). Checked and confirmed: ‘si non magis, certe non minus congruas’ (both negatives kept); ‘non minori necessitate’ = ‘by no lesser necessity’; ‘non optime esse’ negative kept; comparatives latiores/minores in the mean passage. Transcription matches the images.

Conventions: as in the glossary — long s, ligatures and accents normalised, consonantal u → v; speaker abbreviations kept (Ereu., Asphal.); supplied words in [square brackets], Latin of technical terms in [brackets]; the Greek article τῷ kept as printed; marginal notes placed where they stand.
